entities.name: Girolamo Muzio
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Girolamo Muzio (or Mutio Justinopolitano), born in Capodistria (present-day Koper) in 1496 and dying in Padua in 1576, was a prolific Italian humanist, poet, and polemicist whose career spanned the intellectual and religious tumult of the High and Late Renaissance. A staunch advocate for the vernacular Italian language and a zealous defender of Catholic orthodoxy, Muzio engaged directly with the era's most pressing cultural and theological debates. His work is critical for understanding the evolving status of Italian as a literary language and the fierce intellectual battles of the Counter-Reformation.

Muzio's most enduring contribution to Italian letters was his treatise *Battaglie per la difesa dell'italiana lingua* (Battles for the Defense of the Italian Language), published in 1550. In this seminal work, he vigorously argued for the preeminence of the Tuscan dialect as the foundation for a national Italian literary language, challenging the prevailing humanistic reverence for Latin. Beyond linguistic advocacy, Muzio was a formidable polemicist, authoring numerous works against Protestantism, including *Vergerio apostata* (1550) and *Le Mentite Omelie di M. Ochin* (1551), targeting figures like Pier Paolo Vergerio and Bernardino Ochino. His writings also included moral treatises, epistles, and poetry, reflecting his deep immersion in the intellectual currents of Italian courts like Urbino, Ferrara, and Venice.
